migrationNotes: Spine: a cart rolls towards you and you want to predict it. First its velocity after a time, then the distance at a steady velocity, then the average of the two ends when it accelerates, then braking, then the shortcut formula.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): phys-predicting-a-motion-2 (the faded example was dropped to keep the lesson to eleven screens; the worked example and -4 carry the method), -3 (multiple choice, replaced by the numeric phys-predicting-a-motion-double), -5 and -6 stay in the skill check.

lesson.title: Predict the next position

lead.text: Start with the velocity. Say the cart passes the start line at 1 m/s and its acceleration is 3 m/s². An acceleration that stays the same all the way through is called a constant acceleration. The velocity then gains 3 m/s every second: 4 m/s after one second, 7 m/s after two.
Write u for the starting velocity, a for the acceleration and t for the time. The velocity after t seconds is the starting velocity plus the gain per second times the number of seconds.

For t = 2 s that gives 1 + 3 × 2 = 7 m/s. A negative acceleration works the same way. A cart that starts at 9 m/s with a = −2 m/s² has 9 + (−2) × 3 = 3 m/s after 3 s, because each second takes 2 m/s away.

afterFigure.text: The formula tells us how fast the cart is going at the end. How far it has gone is a separate question, and the next few screens deal with it.

lead.text: A cart passes the start line at 3 m/s, and its acceleration stays at 2 m/s² while it runs.

reveal.text: You added the velocity gained each second to the starting velocity: 3 + 2 × 4.

lead.text: The brakes press on, so the acceleration is negative and takes velocity away each second.

On to the second prediction, the distance. Start with the easy case, a velocity that never changes. A cyclist who holds 6 m/s for 5 s covers 6 × 5 = 30 m. That follows from the definition of average velocity. Average velocity is displacement divided by time, so the displacement is the average velocity times the time.
For a trip of 4 seconds at 6 m/s the answer is 24 m, and twice as long gives twice as far. The distance grows in step with the time whenever the velocity stays fixed.

The same idea carries over when the velocity is not steady, as long as we use the right average. An accelerating cart has a different velocity at every moment, so there is no single obvious number to multiply by. Finding that number is the step after this one.
A train runs along a straight track and its velocity never changes.

Now let the velocity change. A cart that starts at 1 m/s and speeds up at 2 m/s² for 4 s ends at 1 + 2 × 4 = 9 m/s, using the formula from earlier. Its velocity was 1 m/s at the start and 9 m/s at the end, and it took every value in between along the way. That leaves a puzzle about which velocity to multiply by the time.

With constant acceleration the velocity rises by the same amount every second, so it moves through its values evenly. The time spent slower than the midpoint is matched by the time spent faster, and the two balance out. The average velocity is the mean of the two ends: (1 + 9) ÷ 2 = 5 m/s. Multiply by the 4 s and the cart has gone 5 × 4 = 20 m.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows both motions covering the same 20 m, which is why the mean of the ends works. It has a limit. The mean of the start and finish velocities is the average only while the acceleration is constant. The sum also needs the finishing velocity, so you will usually find that first, using the formula from the first screen.

cases.label: Starts at 1 m/s, a = 2 m/s², 4 s

steps.headline: A cart starts at 2 m/s and accelerates at 1 m/s² for 6 s. How far does it go?

workedSteps.text: Find the final velocity from v = u + at.
Average the start and the finish.
Distance is average velocity times time.

lead.text: One case turns up often enough to have its own screen: a vehicle braking to a halt. Brakes slow a cart at a steady rate until it stops. The acceleration is constant and negative, and the finishing velocity is 0.

The average of the start and the finish is then half the starting velocity. A cart that brakes from 10 m/s to rest in 5 s has an average velocity of (10 + 0) ÷ 2 = 5 m/s, so it travels 5 × 5 = 25 m before it stops. You do not need to know the acceleration itself. The velocity at each end and the time between them are enough.

afterFigure.text: Real brakes are never perfectly steady, so this is an estimate. For a first look at a stopping distance it is a good one.

lead.text: A cart slows steadily until it stops.

reveal.text: Same method: the average of 12 and 0 is 6 m/s, and that applies for the whole 4 s.

steps.headline: A shortcut and a starting point

lead.text: Putting the pieces together gives a shortcut. The average of u and v = u + at is u + ½at, and multiplying by the time t gives the displacement, which we write s.

Take a cart that starts at 6 m/s with a = 2 m/s² for 3 s. The shortcut gives 6 × 3 + ½ × 2 × 3² = 18 + 9 = 27 m. The two-step method agrees: the cart ends at 12 m/s, averages 9 m/s and goes 9 × 3 = 27 m. The shortcut skips the finishing velocity, but it only holds while the acceleration is constant.
A displacement is a change of position, so to say where the cart ends up you add it to where it began. A cart that starts at the 10 m mark and has a displacement of 27 m finishes at the 37 m mark.

afterFigure.text: From rest, u is 0 and the formula shrinks to s = ½at². The time is squared, so doubling the time makes the cart go four times as far, and tripling it makes the cart go nine times as far. This is why an object that speeds up from rest seems to gather distance faster and faster.

lead.text: A cart starts from rest and speeds up at a constant rate. We only know what it did in its first 2 seconds.

reveal.text: Doubling the time quadruples the distance, so the cart has gone four times 6 m.

lesson.orientation: Use a constant acceleration to predict velocity and displacement.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A cart rolls along a long straight track, and you stand further down it with a stopwatch. You know how fast the cart was going when it passed the start line, and you know it is speeding up at a steady rate. Before it reaches you, you would like to say how fast it will be going in four seconds' time and how far it will have travelled.
Making that kind of prediction is a main use of physics. From a few facts about the present you work out what an object will do next, with no need to wait and watch.

Everything needed is already in hand. We know that velocity changes at a rate called the acceleration, and we know that velocity and time give displacement. This lesson joins the two into a pair of predictions, one for the velocity after a given time and one for the distance covered.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict the velocity and the displacement of a cart that accelerates at a constant rate.

recap.keyIdea: With constant acceleration, v = u + at, and displacement is the mean of the start and finish velocities times the time, which gives s = ut + ½at².

blocks.text: You found that a train at 5 m/s covers 40 m in 8 s. You then used the mean of two velocities to find how far a cart travels while it speeds up or brakes, and saw that from rest, doubling the time quadruples the distance.

recap.nextHook: Gravity is a constant acceleration too. Next we drop a ball and see how far it falls.

questions.prompt: A cart starts at 3 m/s and has constant acceleration 2 m/s² for 4 s. Find its final velocity in m/s.
hints: Find the velocity added during the interval.
Multiply acceleration by time, then add the initial velocity.
Calculate 3 + 2 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: 11 m/s. Constant acceleration adds the same velocity every second: start plus acceleration times time.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds one second's gain only. The cart gains it every second for 4 s.
That is the velocity gained. The cart also started with some velocity.

questions.prompt: Starting at 3 m/s, a cart accelerates at 2 m/s² for 4 s. What is its displacement in metres?
hints: You already have the average velocity from the lines above.
Distance covered is average velocity times time.
Multiply the 7 m/s by the 4 s.
questions.onCorrect: 28 m. Average velocity times time, with the average taken halfway between start and finish.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance if the cart held its starting velocity. It speeds up, so it covers more.
That uses at² without the half. Average the start and finish velocities instead.

questions.prompt: An object starts from rest with constant nonzero acceleration. Doubling the travel time multiplies its displacement by what factor?
hints: Track the exponent on time in ½at².

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Displacement is proportional to time squared; doubling time gives a factor of 2² = 4.

questions.onCorrect: A factor of 4. From rest, displacement grows with time squared, so doubling the time quadruples it.

misconceptions.feedback: Doubling the time also doubles the final velocity, so the distance grows by more than a factor of two.
That would need time cubed. Displacement from rest goes as time squared.

questions.prompt: A cart brakes uniformly from 12 m/s to rest in 4 s. Find its stopping distance in metres.
hints: Uniform braking makes the velocity change linearly.
Average the initial and final velocities.
Multiply (12 + 0)/2 by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Average velocity is (12 + 0)/2 = 6 m/s. Displacement is 6 × 4 = 24 m.

questions.onCorrect: 24 m. Uniform braking makes the average velocity the mean of start and finish; multiply by the time.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the cart as moving at its starting velocity throughout. It slows down, so it goes less far.
That is the average velocity. Multiply it by the time to get a distance.

questions.prompt: A robot begins at x = 5 m with velocity 2 m/s and constant acceleration 1 m/s². Find its position after 4 s, in metres.
hints: First find displacement, then add the initial position.
Use x = x₀ + ut + ½at².
Calculate 5 + 8 + 8.
questions.onCorrect: 21 m. Start position, plus distance from the initial velocity, plus the extra from accelerating.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the extra distance gained by accelerating. Add ½at² as well.
That leaves out the half in ½at². Check the last term.

questions.prompt: When is displacement = ut + ½at² valid for the whole interval?
hints: Identify the assumption used to combine the velocity changes.

acceptedIdeas: When acceleration is constant over the interval
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: This expression assumes constant acceleration during the interval; direction alone is not enough.

choices.label: When acceleration is constant over the interval

questions.onCorrect: Only when acceleration is constant over the interval. That is the assumption the formula is built on.

misconceptions.feedback: Starting from rest is a special case of the formula, not a condition for using it.
The direction of motion does not matter. What matters is that the acceleration stays the same.

questions.prompt: A train moves at a steady 5 m/s for 8 s. How far does it go, in metres?
hints: It covers the same distance every second.
How far does it go in one second?
Multiply that by the 8 seconds.
questions.onCorrect: 40 m. A steady velocity times the time gives the displacement.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the speed and the time. Distance builds up second by second, so multiply.

questions.prompt: A cart moves at 14 m/s and brakes with acceleration −3 m/s² for 4 s. What is its final velocity in m/s?
hints: Braking has a negative acceleration, so each second takes velocity away.
Find the total change in velocity over the whole time.
Add that change to the 14 m/s start.
questions.onCorrect: 2 m/s. A negative acceleration takes the same amount of velocity away each second.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the velocity change as if the cart sped up. The acceleration is negative, so it takes velocity away.
That is the change in velocity only. Add it to the 14 m/s start.

questions.prompt: Why can the mean of the start and finish velocities stand in for the whole trip?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: Constant acceleration changes the velocity steadily.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Constant acceleration changes the velocity steadily.

choices.label: Constant acceleration changes the velocity steadily.

questions.onCorrect: Steady change means the velocity spends equal time above and below the midpoint.

misconceptions.feedback: The velocity does change, from start to finish. The mean works because it changes steadily.
This cart does not start from rest. The mean works for any steady change.

questions.prompt: A cart at 8 m/s accelerates at 2 m/s² for 3 s. Find its displacement in metres.
hints: Find the final velocity first.
Average the starting and finishing velocities.
Multiply that average by the 3 s.
questions.onCorrect: 33 m. Find the final velocity, take the mean with the start, then multiply by the time.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance at the starting velocity. The cart speeds up, so it goes further.
That uses the final velocity for the whole trip. The cart was slower earlier on.

questions.prompt: A cart starts from rest with constant acceleration and covers 6 m in its first 2 s. How far has it gone after 4 s, in metres?
hints: Does the cart go as far in its second 2 s as in its first?
From rest, the displacement depends on the square of the time.
Doubling the time multiplies the distance by 2².

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: From rest s = ½at². Doubling t multiplies s by 2² = 4, so 6 × 4 = 24 m. (Here a = 3 m/s²: ½ × 3 × 4² = 24 m.)

questions.onCorrect: 24 m. From rest, distance grows with the square of the time, so twice the time gives four times the distance.

misconceptions.feedback: Doubling the time doubles the distance only at a steady velocity. This cart speeds up, so the second 2 s cover more ground than the first.
That treats the distance as growing by 6 m for every 2 s. The cart is speeding up, so each later stretch covers more.
